say: You give it a normal variable $X$ and an interval, like $P(X > 512)$. It gives back a **probability** read from the tables.
The key idea: the tables only give the area to the **left** of a $z$-value. Turn $x$ into $z$, look up the left area, then use $1 - P$ or symmetry for anything else.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it every year on Paper 2, usually as a 5 or 10-mark part of the normal distribution question (for example $P(x > 240)$ in 2022), and again inside hypothesis tests.

example.question: The mass of a bag of sugar is normally distributed with mean $500$ g and standard deviation $8$ g. Find the probability that a bag has mass greater than $512$ g.

steps.title: Find the z-score
steps.say: Standardise $512$. Subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation. This gives $\hl{1}{z}$.

steps.title: Look up the left area
steps.say: The tables give $P(z < \hl{1}{1.5})$, the area to the **left**. Find $1.5$ down the side and read across.

steps.title: Use 1 minus the table value
steps.say: We want the area to the **right** of $\hl{1}{1.5}$. The whole area is $1$, so take away $\hl{2}{0.9332}$.

higher.tip: Draw the normal curve and shade the area you want. A relevant diagram earns partial credit, and it stops you using the wrong side of the table.
Write down the mean and the standard deviation first. Naming them earns marks before any calculation.
Write the table value you read, even if you go no further. A probability found directly from the tables earns credit on its own.
Round $z$ to two decimal places before the lookup. A neighbouring table value, like $0.30$ for $0.31$, is accepted.

say: You give it a probability, like the top $20\%$, and the mean and standard deviation. It gives back the **mark** $x$ that fits.
The key idea: this is the tables run backwards. Turn the percentage into a left area, find that area **inside** the table to get $z$, then put $z$ into $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ and solve for $x$.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 2 in most years, as a part of its own worth 5 to 15 marks: find the cut-off for the top or bottom percentage (the oldest $10\%$, the top $10\%$ of marks).

example.question: The marks in an exam are normally distributed with mean $58$ and standard deviation $9$. The top $20\%$ of students get a distinction. Find the lowest mark that gets a distinction, to the nearest whole number.

steps.title: Turn it into a left area
steps.say: Top $20\%$ means $80\%$ of students are below the cut-off. So the left area is $0.8$.

steps.title: Find z inside the table
steps.say: Look **inside** the table for the area closest to $0.8$. Read $\hl{1}{z}$ from the edge.

steps.title: Write the equation in x
steps.say: Put $\hl{1}{0.84}$, the mean and the standard deviation into $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$. Then solve for $\hl{2}{x}$.

steps.title: Round to a whole mark
steps.say: The question wants a whole mark. $65$ would be just short, so round up to $66$.

higher.tip: Say what the percentage means in terms of the left area. Writing that the top $10\%$ is $90\%$ below is work of merit.
Either neighbouring table value is accepted, for example $z = 1.28$ or $1.29$. Pick one and carry on.
Write the equation in $x$ with $z$ in it. It is a step the marks are tied to.
Check the rounding the question asks for. Wrong or missing rounding costs a mark.

say: You give it an angle in degrees or in radians. It gives back the same angle in the **other** unit.
The key idea: $180^\circ = \pi$ radians. To go to radians multiply by $\frac{\pi}{180}$. To go to degrees multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it most years as a step inside bigger parts worth 5 to 10 marks: a sector angle in radians, or a function like $V = 2 - 0.4\cos\frac{\pi}{2}t$ evaluated with the calculator in radian mode.

example.question: A sector of a circle has radius $6$ cm and angle $150^\circ$. (i) Write $150^\circ$ in radians. (ii) Find the area of the sector, in terms of $\pi$.

steps.title: Convert to radians
steps.say: Multiply the angle in degrees by $\frac{\pi}{180}$. Cancel the fraction.

steps.title: Choose the area formula
steps.say: The sector area formula $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ needs $\theta$ in **radians**. Use $\hl{1}{\frac{5\pi}{6}}$, not $150$.

higher.tip: Put the calculator in radian mode when the angle has $\pi$ in it. Using degrees is a named error.
Give the period and the range separately, the right way round. Swapping them costs a mark.
Write the formula with the numbers substituted before you use the calculator. Substitution earns partial credit.
Give the units and round as the question asks. Missing units or wrong rounding costs a mark.

say: You give it any angle, like $240^\circ$ or $210^\circ$. It gives back the **value** of $\sin$, $\cos$ or $\tan$, with the right sign.
The key idea: on the unit circle the point at angle $\theta$ is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. Use the **related angle** to find the size, and the quadrant (CAST) to find the sign.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it a few times as a 5-mark part on either paper: writing a point on a circle as $(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ in 2020, and checking a point such as $(\cos 135^\circ, \sin 135^\circ)$ in 2023.

steps.title: Find the quadrant
steps.say: $210^\circ$ is between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$. That is the third quadrant, where only $\tan$ is positive. So $\cos 210^\circ$ is **negative**.

lines.text: CAST: in the third quadrant, $\sin$ and $\cos$ are both negative.

steps.title: Find the related angle
steps.say: The related angle is the acute angle the line makes with the $x$-axis. In the third quadrant, subtract $180^\circ$.

steps.title: Write the value
steps.say: Take $\cos \hl{1}{30^\circ}$ and put in the **negative** sign from the quadrant.

higher.tip: Draw the unit circle and the angle. The marking notes tell the examiner to check your drawing for work of merit.
State which quadrant the point is in. It is what fixes the sign of $x$ and $y$.
Never write only the answer. A correct answer without work earns only high partial credit.
